findings.who: A widow or widower whose spouse died on active duty in 2024. In 2025 they file as qualifying surviving spouse (or single) and move the family under the military's orders. The filer never served.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether 'you (or, on a joint return, your spouse)' served. This is not a joint return and the filer never served, so a truthful answer is no. The same holds for a spouse filing separately whose member spouse deserted or is imprisoned.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 93, Line 14: 'Use Tax Topic 455 or see Form 3903.' Form 3903 (the cited source; its text is not in the excerpt) lets the spouse and dependents of a member who dies, deserts or is imprisoned deduct the move. The excerpt alone says only 'if you are a member of the Armed Forces on active duty'.
findings.fix: Broaden the gate: 'Since the start of 2022, did you or your spouse (current or deceased, on any filing status) serve in the U.S. armed forces, including the Coast Guard, the reserves or the National Guard?' Or add a separate question: 'In 2025, did you move under military orders as the spouse or dependent of a service member who died, deserted or was imprisoned?'

findings.who: An active-duty Coast Guard member, or a Coast Guard reservist, who made a 2025 permanent-change-of-station move or traveled more than 100 miles for reserve duty.
findings.why_no: The Coast Guard falls under the Department of Homeland Security, not the Department of Defense. A filer may read 'U.S. armed forces, the reserves or the National Guard' as the Department of Defense services only.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 93, Line 14: 'member of the Armed Forces on active duty ... permanent change of station'. Line 12: 'National Guard and reserve members who traveled more than 100 miles from home'.
findings.fix: Name the Coast Guard: 'the U.S. armed forces (Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, Space Force or Coast Guard), their reserves or the National Guard'.

locators: p. 93, Line 12, "Certain business expenses of National Guard and reserve members who traveled more than 100 miles from home"
p. 93, Line 14, "You can deduct moving expenses if you are a member of the Armed Forces on active duty and due to a military order you move because of a permanent change of station"
p. 95, Line 20, "Don’t include any repayments of qualified reservist distributions"

findings.who: A county constable, justice of the peace or coroner who is paid fees for the office and receives no Form W-2. The fees may be collected directly from the public or reported on a Form 1099. The filer (or spouse) has no Form W-2 on the return.
findings.why_no: The computed gate is false whenever no Form W-2 is listed, so the artist/official question is never asked. Fee-basis pay often comes with no W-2.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 93, Line 12: 'Include the following deductions on line 12. ... • Business expenses of fee-basis state or local government officials.'
findings.fix: Do not condition the official branch on a Form W-2. Ask the official part of scope.artist_official on every return. Keep the W-2 condition, if at all, only for the performing-artist branch.

findings.who: A performer who worked as an employee for two or more theater or orchestra employers, but one or both employers wrongly issued a Form 1099 or no form. The filer reports those wages on Form 8919 (or on a Form 4852 substitute) and lists no Form W-2.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed false because no Form W-2 is listed. Yet the filer was an employee performing artist, and the line depends on that fact, not on the form.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 93, Line 12: '• Performing-arts-related expenses as a qualified performing artist.' ... 'For more details, see Form 2106.'
findings.fix: Widen the gate to 'a Form W-2 is listed, or wages are reported on Form 8919 or a substitute W-2 (Form 4852)'. Or ask the artist question whenever there are any wages on line 1a or 1g.

findings.who: An office worker (or the spouse) who also took paid gigs as an employee musician, actor or dancer for two small employers during 2025, with low AGI.
findings.why_no: 'Did you work as a performing artist' reads as a question about occupation. Someone whose main job is something else answers no, though performing-arts services as an employee for two employers can qualify.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 93, Line 12: 'Performing-arts-related expenses as a qualified performing artist.'
findings.fix: Reword: 'In 2025, were you (or your spouse) paid as an employee for any performing-arts work (acting, music, dance, etc.), even as a side job or for only part of the year?'

findings.who: A state or local government employee (not elected or appointed to an office) who is paid a salary plus fees, for example a deputy clerk or registrar who keeps part of the filing fees.
findings.why_no: 'Official' suggests an officeholder. 'Paid from fees' suggests pay made up entirely of fees. A salaried employee who gets fees only in part answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 93, Line 12: '• Business expenses of fee-basis state or local government officials.' (see Form 2106)
findings.fix: Reword: 'In 2025, were you (or your spouse) employed by a state or local government and paid in whole or in part by fees?'

locators: p. 93, Line 12, "Performing-arts-related expenses as a qualified performing artist", "Business expenses of fee-basis state or local government officials"

p. 93, Line 12, "Performing-arts-related expenses as a qualified performing artist", "Business expenses of fee-basis state or local government officials"; p. 93, Line 12, "For more details, see Form 2106"

findings.who: A filer, or their spouse on a joint return, who first bought a limited-partnership or LLC interest, or a stake in a business they do not help run, during 2025. The activity produced a loss or income in 2025, or the interest was bought and sold within 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about 'any year before 2025'. Someone whose first ownership began in 2025 truthfully answers no, so the passive-activity question, and the refusal it leads to, is never reached.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 1: "Form 8582 is filed by individuals, estates, and trusts who have passive activity deductions" and "passive activities include … Trade or business activities in which you did not materially participate for the tax year."
findings.fix: Ask the passive question regardless of the before-2025 gate. Alternatively, widen the gate to 'In 2025 or any earlier year, did you (or your spouse) own or have an interest in …'.

findings.who: A filer who holds units of a publicly traded partnership (MLP) in a brokerage account, or who is a member of a multi-member LLC taxed as a partnership. They receive a Schedule K-1 (Form 1065).
findings.why_no: They read 'a share of a partnership' as a law-firm-style partnership. They think of their holding as stock-like 'units' or as an 'LLC', not a partnership, so they answer no. The Form 8986 question and the passive question are then skipped.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 34, Line 16: "Tax from Form 8978, line 14 (relating to partner’s audit liability under section 6226)"; i8582 p. 1: "passive activities include … Trade or business activities in which you did not materially participate."
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you or your spouse ever receive a Schedule K-1 (Form 1065 or 1120-S), or own an interest in an LLC, a publicly traded partnership (MLP units), a partnership or an S corporation?'

findings.who: A beneficiary of a trust or estate that holds a partnership interest or runs a business. The beneficiary receives a Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) carrying passive income, or a pushed-out Form 8986 through the trust or estate as a pass-through partner.
findings.why_no: A beneficiary does not 'own' a business or 'a share of a partnership', so they truthfully answer the gate no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 34, Line 16: "Tax from Form 8978, line 14 (relating to partner’s audit liability under section 6226)"; i8582 p. 1: "Form 8582 is filed by individuals, estates, and trusts who have passive activity deductions."
findings.fix: Add to the gate: 'or were you a beneficiary of a trust or estate that sent you a Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) or a Form 8986?'

findings.who: A former freelancer, independent contractor, gig worker or rideshare driver who filed Schedule C before 2025. They elected section 179 on equipment such as a vehicle, computer or camera, and part of the deduction was disallowed by the business income limit.
findings.why_no: They do not think of side work as 'owning a business', so they answer the gate no. The section 179 carryover question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 5, Line 10: "The carryover of disallowed deduction from 2024 is the amount of section 179 property, if any, you elected to expense in previous years that was not allowed as a deduction because of the business income limitation."
findings.fix: Reword the gate as 'own or run a business (including self-employment, freelance or gig work reported on Schedule C or F) …'. Alternatively, gate the carryover on 'Did you file Form 4562 for 2024 or any earlier year?'

findings.who: A filer whose before-2025 business interest was held through a single-member LLC or another entity whose name does not match the listed words. Section 179 or passive items flowed to them through that entity.
findings.why_no: They read 'a business, a farm, a rental property, or a share of a partnership or an S corporation' as a complete list of entity types. They think 'I had an LLC', which is none of these, and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 5, Line 6(c): "To report your share of a section 179 expense deduction from a partnership or an S corporation, enter 'from Schedule K-1 (Form 1065)' or 'from Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S)'."
findings.fix: Add help text: 'Count an interest held through an LLC, whether single- or multi-member, and any interest for which you received a Schedule K-1.'

locators: p. 5, Line 10, "The carryover of disallowed deduction from 2024 is the amount of section 179 property, if any, you elected to expense in previous years that was not allowed as a deduction because of the business income limitation" and "If you filed Form 4562 for 2024, enter the amount from line 13 of your 2024 Form 4562" (owner: the printed amount)
, Purpose of Form, "Form 8582 is used by noncorporate taxpayers to figure the amount of any passive activity loss (PAL)"
p. 34, Line 16, "Tax from Form 8978, line 14 (relating to partner’s audit liability under section 6226)"

used.how: pages named by another document's citation

findings.who: A filer who in 2025 held or sold warrants or options to buy shares of a Cayman-organized SPAC or other foreign fund, but never held the shares themselves.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether they 'own shares'. Warrants and options are not shares, so a literal no is truthful.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 114, Line 17p: 'Enter any interest amount from Form 8621, line 16f, relating to distributions from, and dispositions of, stock of a section 1291 fund' (an option to buy PFIC stock is treated as that stock for this purpose).
findings.fix: Ask whether the filer owned shares, or options or warrants to buy shares, of a company or fund set up outside the United States.

findings.who: A beneficiary of a decedent's estate that, during 2025, held foreign fund shares or shares of a foreign company.
findings.why_no: The help lists only a partnership, a trust or a company you own. An estate is not named, and a beneficiary does not 'own' the estate's shares.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 34, Line 16: 'Any tax from Form 8621, line 16e, relating to a section 1291 fund' (this applies to indirect shareholders through estates).
findings.fix: Change the help to 'Count shares held for you, or for anyone you inherit from, by a partnership, an estate, a trust, a pension or another company in which you have an interest.'

findings.who: A filer who holds Nasdaq- or NYSE-listed stock or ADRs in a U.S. brokerage account, where the company is organized in the Cayman Islands, Bermuda or elsewhere abroad. Examples are a SPAC or a Chinese VIE holding company, some of which are PFICs.
findings.why_no: They bought 'U.S. stock' on a U.S. exchange through a U.S. broker. They do not see these as shares of a company 'set up outside the United States', and the carve-out for U.S. funds reinforces that U.S.-traded means domestic.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 34, Line 16: 'Any tax from Form 8621, line 16e, relating to a section 1291 fund'; p. 114, Line 17p: 'Enter any interest amount from Form 8621, line 16f'.
findings.fix: Add help saying: 'This includes stock or ADRs traded on a U.S. exchange if the company is incorporated abroad (for example in the Cayman Islands, Bermuda, Ireland or the British Virgin Islands); check the place of incorporation in the prospectus or on Form 1099-DIV.'

findings.who: A filer, often a returning expat or a U.S. citizen abroad, who holds units of foreign unit trusts, OEICs, SICAVs or similar funds inside a foreign pension, ISA, investment-linked insurance policy or savings wrapper.
findings.why_no: They think they hold 'units' in a pension, account or policy, not 'shares'. A pension or insurance wrapper is not a partnership, a trust or a company they own in their own understanding.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 114, Line 17p: 'Enter any interest amount from Form 8621, line 16f, relating to distributions from, and dispositions of, stock of a section 1291 fund'.
findings.fix: Ask: 'Did you or your spouse own shares or units of a company or fund organized outside the U.S., directly or inside a foreign account, pension, ISA or insurance policy?'

findings.who: An investor in a U.S. private equity, hedge fund or venture partnership, or an S corporation shareholder, where the entity held foreign corporations or foreign funds. The Schedule K-1 reports Form 5471, Form 8992 or Form 8621 items.
findings.why_no: The help asks them to count shares held for them by a partnership, but they do not know what the partnership holds. They answer from their own holdings.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8o: 'Section 951A generally requires that a U.S. shareholder of a controlled foreign corporation include in income its global intangible low-taxed income (GILTI)'; Line 8n: 'include in income its pro rata share of the corporation's subpart F income'.
findings.fix: Add a check the filer can answer: 'Did any Schedule K-1 or statement you received mention a foreign corporation, a PFIC or QEF, Form 5471, Form 8621, Form 8992, subpart F or GILTI?' Count a yes as a yes to the gate.

findings.who: A filer with a fiscal-year or short-year return, or one who disposed of a foreign fund's shares by gift, pledge or transfer early in 2025 and no longer holds them.
findings.why_no: The past tense 'did you own' in 2025 can be read as asking about current or year-end holdings.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 114, Line 17p: interest amount from Form 8621, line 16f, 'relating to distributions from, and dispositions of, stock of a section 1291 fund'.
findings.fix: Ask 'At any time during the tax year, including shares you sold, gave away or otherwise disposed of, did you own...'

locators: p. 34, Line 16, "Any tax from Form 8621, line 16e, relating to a section 1291 fund"; p. 114, Line 17p, "Enter any interest amount from Form 8621, line 16f"

p. 91, Line 8n, "Section 951 generally requires that a U.S. shareholder of a controlled foreign corporation include in income its pro rata share"; p. 91, Line 8o, "Section 951A generally requires that a U.S. shareholder of a controlled foreign corporation include in income its global intangible low-taxed income"

findings.who: A county recorder, constable or justice of the peace paid only from fees collected from the public. No employer issues a W-2, so the return lists no W-2.
findings.why_no: The computed gate counts Forms W-2. With none listed, the tool never asks scope.artist_official and sets it to false. A fee-basis official usually has no W-2, so the parent condition truthfully excludes the very filer the child question covers (same as L-38).
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 93, Line 12: "Business expenses of fee-basis state or local government officials."
findings.fix: Ask scope.artist_official on every return, not only when a W-2 is listed. At minimum, ask the fee-basis official half unconditionally. The qualified performing artist half can stay W-2-gated, since that status requires employee wages from two or more employers.

findings.who: A nonemployee director or independent contractor whose nonqualified deferred compensation failed section 409A. The payer reported it in box 15 of Form 1099-MISC, and the filer has no W-2.
findings.why_no: The gate is true only if a W-2 is listed. The 409A amount can arrive on a 1099-MISC alone, so the gate is false and s2.w2_marks is never asked. The Schedule 2 line 17h tax (20% plus interest) and the refusal it should trigger are both silently dropped.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 114, Line 17h: "This income should be shown in box 12 of Form W-2 with code Z, or in box 15 of Form 1099-MISC."
findings.fix: Gate on 'a Form W-2 or a Form 1099-MISC/1099-NEC is listed', or ask on every return: 'Does any W-2 show code Z in box 12, or any 1099-MISC show an amount in box 15?'

findings.who: A former outside director or consultant who received an excess parachute payment on change of control. It was reported on Form 1099-NEC, and the filer has no W-2.
findings.why_no: No W-2 is listed, so the gate is false. The 20% excess parachute payment tax on Schedule 2 line 17k, and the refusal for it, are never reached.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 114, Line 17k: "If you received a Form 1099-NEC, the tax is 20% of the EPP shown in box 3. Enter this amount on line 17k."
findings.fix: Add a separate, ungated question: 'Did any Form 1099-NEC or W-2 report an excess (golden) parachute payment?' Or widen the gate to include a listed Form 1099-NEC.

findings.who: An employee whose employer never issued a W-2, or issued one the filer lost. The filer reports wages from pay stubs or Form 4852, so no W-2 is listed. The employee may have tips, excess 401(k) deferrals, a statutory-employee job, or NQDC payments.
findings.why_no: The gate counts W-2 documents, not wages. The instructions require reporting earnings without the form, but with zero W-2s listed, all five gated questions are skipped and set to false.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 25, Missing or Incorrect Form W-2?: "Even if you don’t get a Form W-2, you must still report your earnings."
findings.fix: Base the gate on 'had wages as an employee in 2025 (with or without a Form W-2, including a Form 4852 substitute)'. Or first ask 'Did you or your spouse work as an employee in 2025?' and route a yes with no W-2 to the gated questions.

findings.who: A server who received more than $20 a month in cash tips but did not report them all to the employer. The W-2 has nothing in box 8 and no box 12 codes A, B, M or N.
findings.why_no: The gated question asks only whether box 8 or a box 12 code appears. The truthful answer is no, yet Schedule 2 line 5 tax on unreported tips (Form 4137) applies whether or not the employer allocated tips.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 112, Line 5: "If you received tips of $20 or more in any month and you didn’t report the full amount to your employer, you must pay the social security and Medicare or railroad retirement (RRTA) tax on the unreported tips."
findings.fix: Add to the question, or ask separately: 'Did you (or your spouse) receive tips that you did not fully report to your employer, including noncash tips such as tickets?'

findings.who: A filer who left a job in 2024, has no 2025 W-2, and in 2025 received a Form 1099-R (code 8 or P) correcting an excess elective deferral or paying earnings on it.
findings.why_no: No W-2 is listed, so scope.excess_deferral is not asked. Even if it were, its wording ('In 2025, did you put more of your pay ... than the yearly limit') points to current-year deferrals only.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 25, Line 1h: "Corrective distributions from a retirement plan shown on Form 1099-R of excess elective deferrals and excess contributions (plus earnings)."
findings.fix: Also ask, without the W-2 gate: 'Did any Form 1099-R show a corrective distribution of excess deferrals or contributions (box 7 code 8 or P)?' Or include a listed 1099-R with those codes in the gate.

findings.who: A self-employed filer with no W-2 who made elective deferrals to a solo 401(k), alone or together with deferrals at a job held earlier in another year, that exceed the $23,500 limit.
findings.why_no: The gate requires a listed W-2, and the help says 'Box 12 of each W-2 shows the amounts'. A filer whose deferrals were all self-employed salary reductions is never asked, though the limit applies 'under all plans'.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1h: "If the total amount you (or your spouse if filing jointly) deferred for 2025 under all plans was more than $23,500 ... include the excess on line 1h."
findings.fix: Ask whenever there is a W-2 or self-employment income: 'Did you or your spouse make elective (salary-reduction) deferrals to any retirement plan, including a solo 401(k), above the limit?'

findings.who: The beneficiary of a deceased employee, or a former nonemployee director, receiving payments from a nonqualified deferred compensation or nongovernmental 457 plan. The payments are reported on Form 1099-MISC or 1099-R, not a W-2.
findings.why_no: No W-2 is listed, so s1.nqdc_pension is not asked. The question also points only to 'box 11 of any W-2', so a filer holding a 1099 for the same kind of plan would answer no anyway.
findings.irs_text: f1040s1 2025, line 8t: "Pension or annuity from a nonqualifed deferred compensation plan or a nongovernmental section 457 plan"
findings.fix: Ask on every return: 'Did you (or your spouse) receive payments from an employer's nonqualified deferred pay plan or nongovernmental 457 plan, on a W-2, 1099-R or 1099-MISC, including as a beneficiary?' Then classify the answer.

findings.who: A National Guard or reserve member with unreimbursed travel of more than 100 miles for drills.
findings.why_no: scope.artist_official cites Schedule 1 line 12 but names only performing artists and fee-basis officials. A reservist reads the list as complete and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 93, Line 12: "Certain business expenses of National Guard and reserve members who traveled more than 100 miles from home to perform services as a National Guard or reserve member."
findings.fix: If reservists are handled elsewhere, say so in the help. Otherwise add 'or as a National Guard or reserve member who traveled more than 100 miles from home for duty' to the question.

findings.who: A private chauffeur, gardener, yard worker, pool cleaner or estate caretaker paid directly by a family that gave no W-2. The work is done around the home or away from it, not inside it.
findings.why_no: The child question asks only about 'work in someone else's home' and gives indoor examples (nanny, carer, housekeeper). A driver or groundskeeper truthfully answers no because they did not work in the home.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1b: "Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee that was not reported on Form(s) W-2"
findings.fix: Ask: 'Were you (or your spouse) paid by a private household for work in or around its home, or for it personally (for example nanny, carer, housekeeper, cook, gardener, yard worker, private driver, caretaker), with no W-2 for that pay?' Ask the same in the help for the amount.

findings.who: A babysitter or cleaner paid in cash by several families, each under $2,800, with no W-2. They think of this as cash side jobs, not 'wages'.
findings.why_no: The parent question asks about 'wages, tips or strike benefits that are not on a W-2'. Informal cash pay from households is often not seen as wages, so the filer answers no and never reaches the household question.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1b: "An employer isn’t required to provide a Form W-2 to you if they paid you wages of less than $2,800 in 2025"
findings.fix: Do not nest the household question under the wages question. Ask it directly, or add to the parent: 'including cash paid by a family for babysitting, cleaning, caregiving or yard work, even small amounts with no form'.

findings.who: An adult child living with an elderly parent and paid by that parent to be the parent's live-in carer or housekeeper in the shared home, with no W-2.
findings.why_no: 'Someone else's home' reads as excluding a home the filer also lives in. The filer answers no although they are the parent's household employee.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1b: "Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee that was not reported on Form(s) W-2"
findings.fix: Say 'in another person's household, including one you live in (for example a live-in carer, or a household run by a relative)'.

findings.who: A nanny whose employing family gave a W-2 for only part of the year's pay, or a W-2 that understates the pay, or gave a Form 1099-NEC instead of a W-2.
findings.why_no: The question asks about 'a household that gave you no W-2'. A filer who received some form from the family answers no, and the unreported part is dropped.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1b: "Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee that was not reported on Form(s) W-2"
findings.fix: Ask about pay not shown on a W-2: 'Was any of your pay from a household not included on a W-2 (no form, a 1099 instead, or a W-2 for less than you were paid)?' The amount help should say the same.

findings.who: A live-in household worker paid partly in kind (meals, lodging) or in goods, with no W-2.
findings.why_no: The words 'paid' and 'how much were you paid' suggest only cash.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1b: "Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee"
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Include cash and the value of any other pay you received for the work.'

findings.who: A parent is the paid caregiver for an adult disabled son who lives with them. Under a Medicaid waiver, the pay runs through a home-care agency, a managed-care plan or a fiscal intermediary (often 'consumer-directed'). That payer issues the W-2, and box 12 shows code II.
findings.why_no: "did a state Medicaid program pay you": the check and the W-2 name the agency or fiscal agent, not the state. Many caregivers do not know the money is Medicaid waiver funding.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 92, Line 8s: "Your nontaxable Medicaid waiver payments should be reported to you on Form(s) W-2 in box 12, Code II. If nontaxable payments were reported to you in box 1 of Form(s) W-2, report the amount on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1a."
findings.fix: Ask: "In 2025, were you (or your spouse) paid, directly or through a home-care agency, managed-care plan or fiscal agent, under a Medicaid or Medicaid waiver program to care for someone who lived in your home? Answer yes also if any W-2 shows code II in box 12."

findings.who: A caregiver received a W-2 whose box 12 shows code II, and box 1 may be blank or not. They do not know what program funds the pay or what a 'Medicaid waiver payment' is.
findings.why_no: The gate asks for a classification (whether a state Medicaid program paid them) and names no fact they can check on the form. Code II appears only in help text for the gated question, which is never shown after a no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1d TIP: "Your nontaxable Medicaid waiver payments may have been reported to you [on] Form(s) W-2, box 12, with Code II."
findings.fix: Put the code II test in the gate itself: "Does any 2025 Form W-2 for you or your spouse show code II in box 12?" A yes opens the gated questions.

findings.who: A caregiver was paid by Medicaid in 2025 to care for a parent who lived with them. The parent died or moved to a nursing facility in 2025, before the return was prepared.
findings.why_no: "someone who lives in your home" is in the present tense, and no one lives there now. The gated question itself says "lived", but the filer never reaches it.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 92, Line 8s: "Certain Medicaid waiver payments you received for caring for someone living in your home with you may be nontaxable."
findings.fix: Ask: "...to care for someone who lived in your home with you at any time while you were caring for them in 2025 (even if they no longer do)?"

findings.who: An adult child moved into a disabled parent's house to care for them, and Medicaid waiver pay was reported on a W-2 with code II. The caregiver lives in that house too, so it is their home as well.
findings.why_no: The help says "Medicaid pay for care in the other person's own home ... is pay for work in someone's home." The house is the parent's (owned or leased by the parent), so the caregiver reads it as "the other person's own home" and answers no, although they live there with the person cared for.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 92, Line 8s: "Medicaid waiver payments you received for caring for someone living in your home with you"; p. 24, Line 1d TIP: code II on box 12 of Form W-2.
findings.fix: State the test as living together, not ownership: "to care for someone who lived with you, in a home you both lived in, whoever owns or rents it." Limit the help's exclusion to care in a home where the caregiver did not also live.

findings.who: A parent is paid through a Medicaid waiver (for example, a family-caregiver or self-directed program) to care for their own disabled minor or adult child at home.
findings.why_no: They see the money as family support or a program stipend, not as Medicaid paying them 'to care for someone'. They may also read 'someone' as a person outside the family.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 92, Line 8s: "Certain Medicaid waiver payments you received for caring for someone living in your home with you may be nontaxable."
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Includes pay for caring for your own child, parent, spouse or other relative who lives with you, under any Medicaid program, however it is named (waiver, self-directed, family caregiver, IHSS)."

locators: p. 24, Line 1d, "Also enter the total of your taxable and nontaxable Medicaid waiver payments that were not reported on Form(s) W-2, or not reported in box 1 of Form(s) W-2"

p. 24, Line 1d, "Also enter the total of your taxable and nontaxable Medicaid waiver payments that were not reported on Form(s) W-2, or not reported in box 1 of Form(s) W-2"; p. 92, Line 8s, "Your nontaxable Medicaid waiver payments should be reported to you on Form(s) W-2 in box 12, Code II"

p. 92, Line 8s, "Nontaxable amount of Medicaid waiver payments included on Form 1040, line 1a or 1d", "If nontaxable payments were reported to you in box 1 of Form(s) W-2, report the amount on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1a"

findings.who: A high earner whose 2024 Schedule C, farm or K-1 business losses were capped by Form 461. The disallowed excess business loss carries into 2025, yet their 2024 total income was positive (for example, $2M of wages against a $1M business loss).
findings.why_no: The help defines the loss as 'A loss bigger than that year's income'. Their 2024 loss was not bigger than their income, and they think of the amount as a Form 461 disallowance, not as a 'net operating loss'. A truthful no to the definition shown.
findings.line: s1.nol_amount_if_nol (zero instead of the carryover); s1.nol_ebl_if_nol (false, so the refusal it leads to is missed)
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 4, Excess Business Loss: 'Excess business losses that are disallowed are treated as an NOL carryover to the following tax year'; 'This excess business loss of $738,000 will be treated as an NOL carryover to the next tax year.'
findings.fix: Add to the gate and help: 'or did a 2024 Form 461 (excess business loss) disallow part of a business loss?' Drop the claim that the loss must exceed that year's income, or add 'or a business loss limited on Form 461'.

findings.who: A filer (or spouse) whose deductions exceeded income for the first time in 2024, so 2025 is the first year the NOL is used. They never filed Form 172, and their 2024 Form 1040 shows taxable income of zero, not a negative number.
findings.why_no: The help says 'carried forward on an earlier return'. Nothing was carried forward on any earlier return yet, and the 2024 return shows no loss figure at all. They read the question as asking about an NOL they have already been claiming.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 2: 'If you waive the carryback period ... you will have an NOL that can be carried forward ... Start by carrying the NOL to the first tax year after the NOL year.'
findings.fix: Help: 'Including a loss from 2024 that you have not used yet, even if no return has claimed it before. A 2024 return with taxable income of zero and business, rental or disaster losses may have one.' Ask the checkable fact first: 'In 2024 or any earlier year, were your deductions (business, rental, farm, disaster) more than your income?' Then classify.

findings.who: A landlord, a partner or S corporation shareholder with K-1 losses, or a farmer, whose earlier-year rental, pass-through or farm loss produced an unused NOL.
findings.why_no: The help names only 'a business, or ... a disaster or theft with no business'. A rental owner does not see rental property as a business, and a partner sees the loss as the partnership's, not their own.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 1: 'To have an NOL, your loss must generally be caused by deductions from your: • Trade or business, • Work as an employee ..., • Casualty and theft losses resulting from a federally declared disaster, ... or • Rental property'; 'partners or shareholders can use their separate shares of the partnership’s or S corporation’s business income and business deductions to figure their individual NOLs.'
findings.fix: List the sources in the help: 'a business or farm (including your share from a partnership or S corporation K-1), rental property, work as an employee, or a federally declared disaster.'

findings.who: A beneficiary of an estate or trust that terminated in an earlier year with an unused NOL. The NOL passed to the beneficiary on the final Schedule K-1 (Form 1041).
findings.why_no: The beneficiary never had 'a loss bigger than that year's income' on their own return, and nothing was 'carried forward on an earlier return' of theirs. They read the question as about their own losses only.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8a: 'Enter any deduction for an NOL from an earlier year'; i172 p. 1: 'Individuals, estates, and trusts use Form 172 to figure the amount of the NOL that is available for carrying back or forward.'
findings.fix: Add to the help: 'Include an NOL carryover passed to you on a final Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) from an estate or trust that ended.'

findings.who: A divorced or widowed filer, or one now filing jointly with a new spouse, who has a share of an NOL from a joint return with a former spouse, or from separate returns before the current marriage.
findings.why_no: They regard the loss as belonging to the old joint return or to the former spouse, so it is not 'you (or ... your spouse)' as they now read those words.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 3, Change in Marital Status: 'only the spouse who had the loss can take the NOL deduction'; Joint to separate returns: 'figure each of your carryovers separately by separating the NOL portion for each spouse from within the joint return.'
findings.fix: Help: 'Include your share of a loss from a joint return with a former or late spouse.'

locators: p. 91, Line 8a, "Enter any deduction for an NOL from an earlier year"

findings.who: A U.S. citizen who renounced citizenship in 2025, for example at a consulate in October, and lived abroad as a nonresident alien for the rest of the year. Alternatively, a joint filer whose spouse did this.
findings.why_no: The words "not a U.S. citizen" read like a question for immigrants. A former citizen who held citizenship for most of 2025, or who thinks of themselves as an American, may answer no. Nothing in the gate or its help mentions losing or renouncing citizenship during the year.
findings.line: scope.nonresident_if_noncitizen (gated scope.nonresident; a Yes would end the interview). After the no, the tool prepares a full-year Form 1040 for a dual-status filer.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 8: "Most nonresident aliens and dual-status aliens have different filing requirements and may have to file Form 1040-NR."
findings.fix: Ask: "At any time in 2025, were you (or your spouse, on a joint return) not a U.S. citizen? Answer Yes if either of you became a citizen, gave up or lost citizenship, or was never a citizen at any point in 2025." Alternatively, add a separate question: "Did you or your spouse renounce or lose U.S. citizenship, or give up a green card, in 2025?"

findings.who: A filer, or a spouse on a joint return, who naturalized in 2025 without a prior green card, for example through military-service naturalization, and was a nonresident alien before naturalizing.
findings.why_no: The filer is a citizen when filing. They may read the question as present-tense status ("are you a citizen?") and answer no, even though the question says "at any time in 2025".
findings.line: scope.nonresident_if_noncitizen (gated scope.nonresident). The filer was dual-status, but the tool continues as if they were a citizen all year.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 8: "Specific rules apply to determine if you are a resident alien, nonresident alien, or dual-status alien. Most nonresident aliens and dual-status aliens have different filing requirements and may have to file Form 1040-NR."
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Answer Yes if either of you became a U.S. citizen during 2025, even if you are a citizen now."

findings.who: A fiscal-year individual filer whose tax year begins in 2025 and ends in 2026, and who (or whose spouse) gave up citizenship or became a nonresident alien in the 2026 part of that tax year.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about "any time in 2025", calendar year. The change happened in 2026, so the truthful answer is no.
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p. 1 header: "For the year Jan. 1–Dec. 31, 2025, or other tax year beginning , 2025, ending , 20"; i1040gi p. 8 on Form 1040-NR for dual-status aliens.
findings.fix: Ask "at any time during your 2025 tax year". Alternatively, state that the tool handles only calendar-year filers.

locators: p. 8, "Most nonresident aliens and dual-status aliens have different filing requirements and may have to file Form 1040-NR"

findings.who: A union member (or, on a joint return, the spouse) who was locked out by the employer in 2025 and received lockout benefits from the union. There was no strike.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about 'wages, tips or strike benefits'. A locked-out worker was not on strike, and lockout benefits are not wages or tips, so a truthful no is correct as worded.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 24, Line 1h: 'Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts).'
findings.fix: Ask: 'In 2025, did you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) have wages, tips, or strike or lockout benefits from a union that are not on a W-2?'

findings.who: A worker who got a W-2 from a firm that also paid them a bonus, award or non-accountable travel reimbursement on a Form 1099-NEC or 1099-MISC, which should have been wages (Form 8919 reason code H).
findings.why_no: The help gives 'pay from a firm that wrongly treated you as a contractor'. This firm treated them as an employee and gave them a W-2, so they answer no. The gated question 'pay you as an independent contractor, when you believe you were its employee' would also draw a no.
findings.irs_text: f8919 2025 p. 1, Reason code H: 'I received a Form W-2 and a Form 1099-MISC and/or 1099-NEC from this firm for 2025. The amount on Form 1099-MISC and/or 1099-NEC should have been included as wages on Form W-2.'
findings.fix: Add to the gate help and to the gated question: 'or a firm that gave you a W-2 also reported some of your employee pay (such as a bonus or award) on a Form 1099-NEC or 1099-MISC.'

findings.who: A server, valet or hotel worker who reported every cash and card tip to the employer but also got noncash tips such as event tickets, passes or goods.
findings.why_no: The help names only 'tips not reported in full to your employer'. They reported all their tips, and they do not think of tickets as tips that belong on a W-2, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 24, Line 1c: 'Also, include the value of any noncash tips you received, such as tickets, passes, or other items of value. Although you don't report these noncash tips to your employer, you must report them on line 1c.'
findings.fix: Gate help: 'tips you did not report in full to your employer (including tips under $20 a month), or tips that were not money, such as tickets, passes or goods.'

findings.who: A part-time worker who received less than $20 a month in cash tips at a job and so was not required to report them to the employer.
findings.why_no: They read 'tips not reported in full to your employer' as a reporting failure. Because they had no duty to report, they believe nothing applies and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 24, Line 1c: 'This should include any tip income you didn't report to your employer.'
findings.fix: State 'any tips you did not report to your employer, for any reason, including tips you were not required to report.'

findings.who: A gardener, yard worker, pool cleaner or driver paid directly by a household that gave them no W-2, for example less than $2,800 in the year.
findings.why_no: The gate help says 'pay for work in someone's home'. Their work was outside the house or away from it, so they read the example as not covering them. Only the gated question's help names gardeners.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 24, Line 1b: 'Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee that was not reported on Form(s) W-2. An employer isn't required to provide a Form W-2 to you if they paid you wages of less than $2,800 in 2025.'
findings.fix: Gate help: 'pay from a household for work in or around its home (such as a nanny, carer, cleaner, gardener or household driver), even a small amount.'

findings.who: A worker whose U.S. employer never sent a W-2 (for example, a business that closed), or whose W-2 left out part of the wages paid.
findings.why_no: The help examples cover home work, tips and misclassification only. The filer reads that list as complete and answers no. A filer with an incomplete W-2 thinks the wages are 'on a W-2'.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 25, Missing or Incorrect Form W-2?: 'Even if you don't get a Form W-2, you must still report your earnings. If you lose your Form W-2 or it is incorrect, ask your employer for a new one.'
findings.fix: Add to the gate help: 'or wages from any employer that sent no W-2, or a W-2 that leaves out some of your pay.'

findings.who: A U.S. citizen or resident employed by a foreign company, foreign government, embassy or international organization that issues payslips but never a W-2.
findings.why_no: The help examples (home work, tips, misclassification) do not describe ordinary salaried employment abroad. The filer assumes 'not on a W-2' means a missing form from a U.S. employer and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 25, Missing or Incorrect Form W-2?: 'Even if you don't get a Form W-2, you must still report your earnings.'
findings.fix: Add to the gate help: 'including pay from a foreign employer, a foreign government or an international organization, which does not issue W-2s.'

findings.who: A worker treated as a contractor by an individual, a nonprofit or a state agency, or paid through a third party rather than by the business they worked for.
findings.why_no: The help and the gated question say 'a firm' and 'did a firm pay you'. They do not see an individual or a public body as a 'firm', or the payer was not the business they served, so they answer no.
findings.irs_text: f8919 2025 p. 2, Firm: 'the term "firm" means any individual, business enterprise, company, nonprofit organization, state, or other entity for which you performed services. This firm may or may not have paid you directly for these services.'
findings.fix: Say 'a business, person, nonprofit or government body you worked for (whether it paid you directly or through someone else).'

findings.who: A filer who itemized for 2023 and took the standard deduction for 2024. In 2025 they receive insurance money for a 2023 casualty loss, or a refund of 2023 real property tax.
findings.why_no: The help says: 'If you took the standard deduction for 2024, money back for something you could deduct only by itemizing is not income: answer No.' The filer did take the standard deduction for 2024 and follows the help, but the recovered item was itemized in 2023.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 27, Worksheet 2: 'If you recovered amounts from more than 1 year, such as a state income tax refund from 2024 and a casualty loss reimbursement from 2023, complete a separate worksheet for each year. Use information from your tax return for the year the expense was deducted.' p. 24: 'If you didn't itemize deductions for the year for which you received the recovery...'
findings.fix: Tie the help to the year of the deduction: 'If you took the standard deduction for the year you deducted the item, money back for something you could deduct only by itemizing is not income.' Better, drop the year test from the gate and ask it after a Yes.

findings.who: A filer who itemized for 2022 or 2023. In 2025, after a state amended return or audit, they receive a state income tax refund for that earlier year.
findings.why_no: The gate excludes any 'state or local income tax refund' with no year limit, and says such refunds are 'asked about separately'. A truthful No follows. The 2024-focused state refund question may not route a pre-2024 refund to refusal.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24, Itemized Deduction Recoveries: 'must use this discussion if ... 1. You received a refund in 2025 that is for a tax year other than 2024.' p. 27, Worksheet 2: 'complete a separate worksheet for each year.'
findings.fix: Narrow the exclusion to 'other than a refund of 2024 state or local income tax', or confirm that the separate state refund question asks the year of the refund and refuses for a year other than 2024.

findings.who: A filer whose earlier-year deduction or credit did not lower that year's tax but did increase a carryover, such as an NOL or an unused credit carried forward. In 2025 the amount is refunded or repaid.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether the deduction or credit 'lowered your tax'. That year's tax was zero either way, so the filer answers No truthfully. The tax benefit rule counts the larger carryover as having reduced tax.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24, Tax benefit rule: 'any increase to an amount carried over to the current year that resulted from the deduction or credit is considered to have reduced your tax in the earlier year.'
findings.fix: Ask the checkable fact: 'In 2025, did you or your spouse get money back, or a credit or price reduction, for something you deducted or took a credit for on an earlier year's return?' Apply the tax benefit test after a Yes.

findings.who: A filer who deducted an item in an earlier year but cannot tell whether the deduction changed their tax. Examples: tax computed with the capital gain worksheet, AMT, or credits that already brought tax near zero.
findings.why_no: The words 'whose deduction or credit ... lowered your tax' require a refigured prior-year computation. Unsure, the filer answers No, and the refusal the gated lines lead to is skipped.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 25, Capital gains: 'you'll have to refigure your tax for the earlier year to determine if the recovery must be included in your income'; p. 28, Subject to AMT: 'you'll have to refigure your tax for the earlier year'.
findings.fix: Remove 'lowered your tax' from the gate. Ask only whether money, a credit, or a price reduction came back for a previously deducted or credited item.

findings.who: A filer who claimed a credit on an item and later got a downward price adjustment or manufacturer rebate. Or one whose earlier-year property tax refund was applied as a credit against the next bill instead of paid in cash.
findings.why_no: 'Paid back' suggests cash returned to the filer. A price adjustment, or a credit applied to a later bill, does not read as being 'paid back'.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 28, Amounts Recovered for Credits: 'You had a recovery if there was a downward price adjustment or similar adjustment on the item for which you claimed a credit.' p. 24: 'The most common recoveries are refunds, reimbursements, and rebates'.
findings.fix: Say 'paid back, refunded, reimbursed, credited, or given a rebate or price reduction'. Add a credit example to the gate's help, such as a rebate on an item you took an energy or vehicle credit for.

findings.who: A filer who took the standard deduction for 2024 and in 2025 recovers a nonitemized deduction. Examples: a payment on a bad debt deducted in an earlier year, a refund of an earlier year's deducted business or self-employed expense, or a returned penalty on early withdrawal of savings.
findings.why_no: All of the gate's examples are itemized deductions (property tax, mortgage interest, medical bill). The help then says a standard deduction filer should 'answer No'. The filer reads the examples as the whole rule and the standard-deduction sentence as covering them.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24: 'You may also have recoveries of nonitemized deductions (such as payments on previously deducted bad debts)'; p. 28: 'If you recover an amount that you deducted in an earlier year when you were figuring your AGI, you must generally include the full amount of the recovery in your income'.
findings.fix: Add nonitemized and credit examples to the gate's help (a repaid bad debt, a refunded business expense, a rebate on a credited item). State that the standard-deduction rule applies only to itemized-only items, and that other deductions and credits still count.

findings.who: A filer who deducted general sales tax for 2024 using actual receipts, or the table plus a large purchase. In 2025 they return an item and get its sales tax refunded.
findings.why_no: They think of the refund as part of a store return, not as money 'paid back' for a deduction. A table user may also think no specific tax was deducted. The gate's examples do not mention sales tax.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24, Example 27: 'In 2025, you return an item you had purchased and receive a $500 sales tax refund... The maximum refund that you may have to include in income is $500'.
findings.fix: Add to the gate's help: 'a refund of sales tax on an item you returned, if you deducted sales tax for that year'.

locators: p. 24, Example 27, "The maximum refund that you may have to include in income is $500 because it’s less than the excess of the tax deducted"
p. 24, Recoveries, "A recovery is a return of an amount you deducted or took a credit for in an earlier year"

p. 24, Recoveries, "You may also have recoveries of nonitemized deductions (such as payments on previously deducted bad debts) and recoveries of items for which you previously claimed a tax credit"; p. 25, Caution, "If you also recovered an amount deducted as a nonitemized deduction, figure the amount of that recovery to include in your income and add it to your adjusted gross income (AGI) before applying the rules explained here"

p. 27, Worksheet 2, "complete a separate worksheet for each year. Use information from your tax return for the year the expense was deducted"

findings.who: An office worker, cook or counselor at a church-run seminary, camp, retirement home, mission board or denominational agency who knows the employer only as a nonprofit. The W-2 shows wages in box 1, but boxes 4 and 6 are empty because the employer filed the church election.
findings.why_no: They do not know the employer is 'a church or other religious body' or is one 'a church controls'. The help names only a school, hospital or charity. The decisive fact, a W-2 with no social security or Medicare tax withheld, is not asked until after the gate.
findings.irs_text: i1040sse p. 1: "Church employee income is wages you received as an employee ... of a church or qualified church-controlled organization that has a certificate in effect electing an exemption from employer social security and Medicare taxes"
findings.fix: Widen the gate to cover a fact the filer can check: 'or did you (or your spouse) get a Form W-2 with wages in box 1 but boxes 4 and 6 (social security and Medicare tax withheld) empty?' Also widen the help to 'any organization a church or denomination controls, such as a seminary, camp, retirement home, mission board or agency'.

findings.who: A member of a Catholic or other religious order who has not taken a vow of poverty (a lay brother, sister or associate). The order assigns them to work for an outside, non-religious employer that pays them.
findings.why_no: They are not 'clergy (a minister, priest, rabbi or imam)', and their payer is not 'a church or other religious body'. The gate never mentions members of religious orders, even though the gated question does.
findings.irs_text: i1040sse p. 1: "you must pay SE tax on salaries and other income for services you performed as a minister, member of a religious order who hasn’t taken a vow of poverty, or Christian Science practitioner"
findings.fix: Add to the gate: 'or are you (or your spouse) a member of a religious order, whoever paid you'. Add the order member to the help text.

findings.who: A minister or order member whose 2025 compensation was mainly or entirely in kind (a parsonage, utilities, meals and lodging), or love offerings and gifts from congregants, with little or no cash salary.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether they were 'paid for work'. They see housing and personal offerings as support or gifts, not pay.
findings.irs_text: i1040sse p. 1: "Also, include on line 2: • The rental value of a home or an allowance for a home furnished to you (including payments for utilities); and • The value of meals and lodging provided to you, your spouse, and your dependents"
findings.fix: Reword the gate to 'paid, or given housing, a housing allowance, meals, lodging or offerings, for work ...'. Alternatively, ask first whether the filer or spouse is clergy or a religious-order member, whatever the form of pay.

findings.who: A self-employed religious officiant with a title outside the parenthetical list, such as a licensed or commissioned minister, pastor, deacon, cantor, swami or pandit. Families, not a congregation, paid this person directly for weddings, funerals or ceremonies.
findings.why_no: The payer was not 'a church or other religious body'. The officiant reads 'clergy (a minister, priest, rabbi or imam)' as a complete list of titles that does not include theirs.
findings.irs_text: i1040sse p. 1: "you must pay SE tax on salaries and other income for services you performed as a minister"
findings.fix: Change the parenthetical to 'clergy of any faith or title (for example, a minister, pastor, priest, deacon, cantor, rabbi or imam), including fees paid directly by individuals for weddings, funerals or other services'.

findings.who: A fiscal-year filer who is clergy or a church employee, whose tax year began in 2025 and runs into 2026, with the religious work or pay falling in 2026.
findings.why_no: 'In 2025' reads as the calendar year, not the tax year.
findings.irs_text: i1040sse p. 3: "If your tax year is a fiscal year, use the tax rate and annual earnings limit that apply at the time the fiscal year begins."
findings.fix: Say 'During your 2025 tax year' instead of 'In 2025'.

findings.who: A filer who leases a car, or rents equipment such as a camera rig or trailer, from someone else and rents it on to others in 2025 (for example a leased car listed on Turo, or rented tools sublet to a contractor). The filer earns rent from personal property they do not own.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether they rented out 'anything you own'. They own nothing they rented out, so a truthful answer is No.
findings.line: scope.rent_personal_if_rental (the refusal for personal-property rental is never reached)
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 5, Personal property: "Do not use Schedule E to report income and expenses from the rental of personal property, such as equipment or vehicles." The rule turns on renting personal property, not on owning it.
findings.fix: Drop 'you own' or broaden it: "...rent out, sublet, or offer for rent anything, whether you own it, lease it, or rent it from someone else..."

findings.who: A cash-basis filer who rented equipment or a vehicle to someone in late 2024 and received the rent in January 2025. Nothing was rented or offered for rent during 2025.
findings.why_no: 'In 2025, did you ... rent out, or offer for rent' asks about the rental activity in 2025, not about rent received in 2025, so a truthful answer is No.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 5, Personal property: rental of personal property is not reported on Schedule E but on Schedule C or Schedule 1, lines 8l and 24b. Rent received in 2025 is 2025 income regardless of when the rental occurred.
findings.fix: "In 2025, did you ... rent out or offer for rent anything, or receive any rent or royalties (including rent for an earlier year)?"

findings.who: A filer who rents out personal items such as camera gear, costumes, tools, a boat, an RV, a jet ski or a bike. None of these is a house, a room, land, or (to them) a 'vehicle'.
findings.why_no: The help lists only real estate: "A house, an apartment, a room, land or a vacation home counts". The filer reads it as the whole scope and concludes the question is about real estate.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 5, Personal property: "rental of personal property, such as equipment or vehicles"; the business test ("primary purpose ... income or profit ... continuity and regularity") and the non-business routing to Schedule 1 lines 8l and 24b.
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Renting out any belongings counts too, such as a car, boat, RV, trailer, tools, camera gear or other equipment, including through an app such as Turo."

findings.who: A filer who earns money from car-sharing apps, or who supplies equipment for a fee as part of a service (a photo booth, DJ gear, a bounce house, a party-rental item delivered and set up).
findings.why_no: They think of the income as 'sharing' or as pay for a service, not as renting something out, and answer No.
findings.irs_text: i1040se (2025) p. 5, Personal property: "Do not use Schedule E to report income and expenses from the rental of personal property, such as equipment or vehicles."
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Count money from car-sharing or peer-to-peer rental apps, and fees for letting others use your equipment, even when you also provide a service with it."

locators: p. 5, Personal property, "Do not use Schedule E to report income and expenses from the rental of personal property, such as equipment or vehicles"

findings.who: A striking worker paid weekly benefits by a strike fund that is not a union, such as a labor council solidarity fund, a worker-run or crowdfunded strike fund, or another organization's hardship fund. The payments required picket duty or went to every striker regardless of need.
findings.why_no: The gated helper and the input both ask about benefits 'from a union'. The payer was not their union, so a truthful no follows and the input is never reached.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1h: 'Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts)' with no limit on who pays them
findings.fix: Ask: 'In 2025, did you (or, on a joint return, your spouse) get strike or lockout benefits from a union, strike fund or any other source (in cash or in kind)?' Remove 'from a union' from the input as well.

findings.who: A worker who was locked out by the employer and did not strike. The worker got lockout benefits from the union and no Form W-2 shows them.
findings.why_no: The parent gate asks only about 'wages, tips or strike benefits that are not on a W-2'. A lockout is not a strike and the payments were not wages, so the worker answers no at the parent. The child question that names lockout benefits is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1h: 'Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts)'
findings.fix: Ask the strike or lockout question directly rather than behind the pay-not-on-W-2 parent. At minimum, change the parent to 'wages, tips, or strike or lockout benefits that are not on a W-2'.

findings.who: A striker whose union paid a flat weekly amount to every member on the picket line. The union called it 'assistance' or 'support', and no form was issued.
findings.why_no: The question says 'other than bona fide gifts' and the help says 'Leave out true gifts'. The filer treats the union's help as a gift and answers no, or enters zero. Benefits conditioned on picketing or paid without regard to need are not bona fide gifts.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1h: 'Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts)' must be included in the total on line 1h
findings.fix: Ask about facts the filer can check: did you get any money or goods from a union or strike fund during a strike or lockout? Then classify with factual questions, such as whether the payments required picket duty or were paid to members regardless of need. Treat them as taxable unless they were based only on need with no conditions.

findings.who: A striker whose union or strike fund gave groceries or food vouchers, or paid the striker's rent or utilities directly to the landlord or utility, instead of paying cash.
findings.why_no: The words 'How much did you get' and the parent's grouping with 'wages, tips' suggest cash pay. The filer does not see in-kind support or third-party payments as benefits they 'got' and enters zero or answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1h: 'Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts)'
findings.fix: Add help: 'Include the value of food, vouchers, and rent or bills paid for you, not only cash.'

locators: p. 24, Line 1h, "Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts)"
p. 24, Line 1h, "The following types of income must be included in the total on line 1h", "Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts)"

findings.who: A restaurant server or hotel concierge, or the spouse on a joint return, is paid on a W-2 and reports every cash and card tip to the employer, so W-2 box 7 shows those tips. In 2025 customers also gave them event tickets, passes or a gift card worth a few hundred dollars.
findings.why_no: The parent question asks about 'wages, tips or strike benefits that are not on a W-2'. This filer's wages and tips do appear on the W-2, so they answer no. They do not see that noncash tips are never on a W-2. The noncash-tip question sits only under this parent, so the filer never reaches the words 'tips that were not money'.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1c: 'Also, include the value of any noncash tips you received, such as tickets, passes, or other items of value. Although you don't report these noncash tips to your employer, you must report them on line 1c.'
findings.fix: Do not reach the noncash-tip question only through the 'not on a W-2' parent. Either ask it on its own for every filer with W-2 wages, or add to the parent's words and help: 'including tips that were not money, such as tickets, passes or other items of value. These are never on a W-2, even when all your other tips are.'

findings.who: A tipped employee, such as a valet, bartender or tour guide, whose customers gave them concert tickets, sports passes, a bottle of wine or a gift card in place of or on top of money.
findings.why_no: To this filer, 'tips' means cash or card tips. They think of items from customers as gifts, not tips or pay. So at both the parent question and the child question ('cash or card tips ... not reported in full ... or tips that were not money') they answer no, or they stop reading after the cash-tip part.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1c: 'include the value of any noncash tips you received, such as tickets, passes, or other items of value'
findings.fix: Ask noncash tips as a separate yes/no question with its own wording: 'Did customers give you (or your spouse) anything other than money for your service at a job, such as tickets, passes, gift cards or other items of value? These count as tips even if you think of them as gifts.' Keep it apart from the question on unreported cash tips.

findings.who: A parent or representative files the final 2025 return for a 17-year-old who died in mid-2025 and had $5,000 of interest and dividends. A parent of the child was alive at the end of 2025.
findings.why_no: The helper says 'You were under 24 at the end of 2025'. The child was not alive at the end of 2025, so the person filing may read the question as not applying and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1, Who Must File: 'The child either: a. Was under age 18 at the end of 2025 ... 4. At least one of the child's parents was alive at the end of 2025.'
findings.fix: Add help text: 'If you are filing for someone who died during 2025, answer for their age on the date of death.' Or ask for the date of birth (and date of death, if any) and compute the age.

findings.who: A parent uses the tool to prepare their 16-year-old child's own single return. The child has $4,000 of capital gain distributions.
findings.why_no: The parent reads 'You were under 24' as asking about themselves, the person typing, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1, Who Must File: 'Form 8615 must be filed for any child who meets all of the following conditions. 1. The child had more than $2,700 of unearned income.'
findings.fix: Ask 'Was the person this return is for (the taxpayer named on line 1) under 24 at the end of 2025?' Or compute the age from a date of birth the tool already collects.

findings.who: A full-time student aged 19 to 23 whose scholarship or fellowship grant exceeded tuition and required fees, for example $6,000 used for room and board, and was not reported on a Form W-2. A parent is alive and the student has little earned income.
findings.why_no: The question's examples are all investment income ('interest, dividends or gains from investments'). The student does not think of a scholarship as income at all, and certainly not as investment income, so the student answers no.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1, Unearned Income: "It includes ... taxable scholarship and fellowship grants not reported on Form W-2"
findings.fix: Name every kind of unearned income in the question and help: "...income that was not pay for work, such as interest, dividends, capital gains (including fund distributions), rents, royalties, the taxable part of a scholarship or fellowship grant not on a Form W-2, unemployment compensation, alimony, pension, IRA or annuity distributions (including inherited IRAs), the taxable part of social security, or trust or estate distributions?"

findings.who: A filer under 24 who inherited an IRA or 401(k), for example from a grandparent, and took $8,000 in distributions in 2025, which a Form 1099-R reports. A parent is alive.
findings.why_no: An inherited retirement distribution is neither pay for work nor 'interest, dividends or gains from investments' as the filer understands those words, and the filer sees it as an inheritance.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1, Unearned Income: "It includes ... pension and annuity income ... and income (other than earned income) received as the beneficiary of a trust"
findings.fix: List retirement distributions (IRA, pension, annuity, including inherited accounts) and trust or estate distributions (Schedule K-1) in the question, or ask about each kind separately and add them up.

findings.who: A minor or student under 24 who received taxable unemployment compensation, or a child receiving survivor or dependent social security benefits with a taxable part, together with other unearned income totaling more than $2,700.
findings.why_no: Unemployment benefits feel like a replacement for wages, and social security benefits feel like a benefit rather than income. Neither matches the investment examples, so the filer leaves them out of the total.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1, Unearned Income: "It includes ... unemployment compensation, alimony, the taxable part of social security and pension payments"
findings.fix: State explicitly that unemployment compensation and the taxable part of social security count, and tell the filer to add all such amounts together.

findings.who: A child under 18 whose UTMA or UGMA custodial account, held under the child's SSN and managed by a parent, earned $3,500 in dividends and capital gain distributions that were reinvested. Alternatively, a filer under 24 who receives rent or royalty income from property held for them.
findings.why_no: The filer thinks of the custodial account as the parent's money, or reinvested dividends as not 'had'. Rents and royalties are not among the investment examples. Any of these leads the filer to say they had no such income.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1, Unearned Income: "It includes taxable interest, dividends, capital gains (including capital gain distributions), rents, royalties"
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Count income from accounts held in your name or SSN even if a parent or custodian manages them, including reinvested dividends and fund capital gain distributions, and rents or royalties."

findings.who: A filer with several small kinds of unearned income, for example $1,500 of interest, $900 of dividends and $600 of capital gain distributions, none above $2,700 alone but $3,000 in total.
findings.why_no: The question does not say to add the kinds together. A filer checks each Form 1099 against $2,700 and finds none above it.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1, Who Must File: "The child had more than $2,700 of unearned income"
findings.fix: Ask for the total: "Adding together all of these kinds of income, was the total more than $2,700?" Or collect the amounts and compute the comparison.
